subject: understanding C++ optimizations -- extra code runs faster

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: understanding C++ optimizations -- extra code runs faster
parts:
I'm getting a very repeatable effect that
the method on var objects written as:

double adjoint() const {
if (is_constant())
return 0.0;
return adjoints[node_];
}

is faster (by about 1.5% to 2.5%) than the version
without the test.

double adjoint() const {
return adjoints[node_];
}

Any ideas as to what might be going on? There are
a couple of other similar tests that have the same
behavior. I'm baffled.

I'd always believed the old adage that "the fastest
code is the code that doesn't run at all".

I can't seem to reproduce the huge diff I thought I
saw with const vs. not in:

inline var dot(const Eigen::Matrix<var,1,Eigen::Dynamic>& a,
const Eigen::Matrix<var,1,Eigen::Dynamic>& b);

It did just dawn on me in trolling through their code that
you can have different implementations for const and non-const
returns (either a ref or const ref, just like for std::vector).

- Bob

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] understanding C++ optimizations -- extra code runs faster
parts:
A well predicted branch could be cheaper than indirect memory access.
Computing adjoints[node_] involves fetching node_ (whose location is
known and can be prefetched) and then fetching adjoints[node_] (whose
location is not). is_constant() only requires a single fetch from a
known location, so might be easier to pipeline. Could be some
speculative evaluation going on as well—if is_constant() turns out to
be true, then you can just keep going and don't stall waiting to get
adjoints[node_].

This is, of course, all highly speculative. But none of it is
inconsistent with the adage—it's much faster not to run "return
adjoints[node_];".

Matt
